The county can’t spend a dollar, sign a contract, settle a claim, or move budget money without its Legislature voting on a numbered resolution. The county ledger shows where the money went — this register is the record of who voted to send it. Every row links back to the county’s own source document.

The money · what the votes put dollars behind

The largest permissions on record

482 of the 5,871 resolutions carry a “not to exceed” ceiling. They are deliberately never summed into one headline number: change orders restate a whole contract’s total as the work changes, refunding bonds reissue existing debt, and the biggest figures are IDA bond issues the county approves but never spends. So this page shows the permissions themselves, biggest first, each labeled for what it is — and the county ledger shows what was actually spent.

How this register is built

The record, verified against itself

Sources. The Niagara County Legislature publishes agendas, resolution packets, and meeting minutes for every session at niagaracounty.gov. This register parses the 2015–2026 era — the years where full resolution texts and minutes are posted. Meetings from 2007–2014 are on the county site as agenda lists only, so they are deliberately excluded rather than shown half-built.

The tie-out. Each meeting’s agenda prints its own list of resolution numbers. Every parsed resolution is checked against that list; the parse of a meeting fails loudly rather than publishing a partial read.

What a machine cannot read. Of the 5,871 resolutions, 392 sit in meetings whose posted minutes are scanned images with no text layer, 109 in meetings where the county has not posted minutes at all, and 0 on agendas for meetings not yet held. Against the minutes a machine can read, 5,117 of 5,370 votes are matched (95%). 13 documents the county’s site no longer serves were recovered from the Internet Archive’s crawl of niagaracounty.gov; their source links point to the archived copies. Nothing here is OCR-guessed — where the record is an image, this register says so and links it.

Honesty notes. The county’s PDFs carry a machine text layer with light OCR noise (“CmTied” for “Carried”, the digit 1 read as the letter I); parsing tolerates the known artifacts and otherwise reports what is printed, including vote totals that occasionally disagree with the chamber’s seat count. Dollar figures are read from the resolution text: “up to” amounts are authorization ceilings, other figures are amounts mentioned in the text (bid tabulations include losing bids) — neither is a payment record. Votes shown as unmatched simply were not found by the parser in that meeting’s minutes; the minutes remain the authority.
